en: The Scripture on Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into the Dharmakāya, Spoken by the Buddha as the Ratnakūṭa Samādhi,
translated by the Anxi Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī went to where the Buddha was and stood outside the gate.
Why was this? The Buddha sat in samādhi;
not long after, he awoke and beheld Mañjuśrī.
He was then invited to enter, prostrated himself, and stood before him.
The Buddha said,
"Please be seated."
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha,
"What is the name of this samādhi you have just entered?
The Buddha replied:
"Ratnakūṭa," Mañjuśrī asked again,
"For what reason are you named Ratnakūṭa?"
The Buddha said:

"It is like a maṇi jewel that is inherently pure and fine; when it is further washed with water and placed on level ground, it becomes even more brilliant and transparent, such that there is no one who does not see it."

Entering the samādhi to which he belonged, he beheld countless, asankhyeya buddha-fields and Buddhas in the eastern direction; yet these all subsequently vanished. Abiding within this samādhi, there was no fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of all phenomena that he did not perceive.
Those who have faith consider this to be obtaining the seal; whatever they say accords with the truth.
The mani-jewel pavilion has four corners; looking from one corner, one sees all the corners without any deficiency, and thus one perceives all fundamental limits.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī,
"Do you know the limit of beginning? He replied:
“I know. “What is it that you know? He replied:

"What I abide in is the ultimate limit (*koṭi*); those who desire various things have a different limit. One who abides in this limit neither exists within phenomena (*dharma*) nor within good or evil; all phenomena are likewise so."
Those who know this understand it through careful examination.
As for all who possess knowledge, they do so by means of "knowing nothing," transmitted from the origin through successive practice; there is no creator, and therefore there is no bottom limit.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī,
"What is meant by this wisdom?
[Mañjuśrī replied,] "To examine this thoroughly is what constitutes wisdom."
He asked again:
"What is the mindfulness of the path called 'the path'? He replied:
"The path that is contemplated is non-contemplation; therefore, it is called the 'path'.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"If one speaks of non-contemplation by means of contemplation, with what dharma should one instruct new learners, whether men or women?"
Mañjuśrī said:

“There is nothing that emerges, nor is there anything to be liberated from. Lust, anger, and delusion are without limit; it is by means of these dharmas that all beings are taught. Because they have no root, they cannot emerge and cannot be liberated.”
To say, "I can destroy the primordial limit," is to say one cannot;
to say, "I can sever birth," is likewise impossible.
One who does not abandon worldly affairs and does not contemplate the proximity of the Way—such a person may indeed be taught as an ordinary man.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha,
"By means of what dharma do you teach and train?
The Buddha said:
"What I teach does not destroy form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; there is nothing to be destroyed.
Nor do I teach the destruction of lust, anger, and delusion, so as to cause one to attain incalculable dharmas."
"By means of these teachings, those who practice the path to Buddhahood shall, for this reason, personally attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:

"One attains Buddhahood because there is no dharma to be destroyed; one can become a Buddha because there is no dharma to be obtained. A Buddha is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya); all the various powers (bala) and fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya) are entirely entries into the Dharma-body."
Why is this so? Because it is impossible to divide the one body into a dharma-body; the dharma-body is without number.
For what reason?
One does not say that this is an ordinary person or that this is an extraordinary person; for the *dharmakāya* is equal and without distinction. That which has no dispersed body is the *dharmakāya*.

It is like the four great rivers all returning to the sea, merging into a single flavor; just as various names for phenomena are unified as the one *dharmakāya*, so too do all the various seeds each have their own name, yet when they are gathered and assembled together, they are called "grain."
Whether mundane matters or matters of the Way, they are all unified as the single Dharma-body. Why is this so?

It cannot be pointed out as being mundane matters, nor can matters of the Way be described; this body of mundane matters is itself the Dharma-body, and it cannot be seen or perceived, just as I have explained the Dharma-body.
"Whoever possesses faith and the two types of knowledge will completely eliminate all the evil they have committed.
Mañjuśrī said:

"Regarding the Dharma-body, one does not perceive it being born in the heavens, nor does one perceive it among humans, nor does one perceive it within the three realms of existence, nor does it abide in nirvāṇa."
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“What you have just said is indeed so.
If someone were to ask you, [you would say that] the Buddha has taught that there are five destinies.”
"How should one explain this?

Mañjuśrī replied, "It is like a person who, while lying in bed, sees himself entering hell, or becoming a bird or beast, or a hungry ghost (preta), or ascending to the heavens, or being among humans; yet upon waking, he sees nothing at all."
That Dharma-body is without attachment.
Why is this? Because it exists merely as a designation.
Those who calculate fall into the mundane; from Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas up to the Buddhas, they are all equal in the single Dharma-body. Why is this?
Because it is impossible to differentiate them.
For example, various kinds of jewels can be distinguished and known, yet the Dharma-body cannot be distinguished. Why is this?
Because it is undifferentiable, and because it is without birth and without death.
The Dharma-body is neither produced nor extinguished.
Why is this? Because it is eternally abiding.
There is neither defilement nor purity.
Why is this? Because there is no one who transgresses, nor is there anyone who is liberated, nor anything from which one is liberated.
The Buddha, who knows all things, further asked Mañjuśrī,
“Do you know the Dharma-body?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"If one attains it, it can be known.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī:
"Do you know the location where the world resides?"
He replied, "I know.
The Buddha said:
Mañjuśrī said: “As for what that is:

when a manifested person dwells in the world, being in this world, there is only a name sought as thin as a hair-tip; yet there is no one who speaks it for me, and that world likewise does not depart from the Dharmakāya.”
The Buddha asked again:
"Where does the world abide?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"It is, for example, like a cloud: it has no location and yet is not non-existent; it is neither weak nor strong. This is the characteristic of the world from age to age.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī, "Do you think that I am extinguished?"
Mañjuśrī said: "No. Why is that? Because..."
“The Dharma-body has no arising; if there were arising, there would be cessation.
Because the Dharma-body does not arise, one knows that the Buddha does not cease.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī:
"If you hear that all the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who have already passed away have entered parinirvāṇa,
would you believe it? He replied,
"I believe it."
The Buddha asked,
"What is faith? Mañjuśrī replied:
“Those Buddhas are all emanations created by the Buddha; they believe in them because they have manifested parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha asked Mañjuśrī:
“Do you see, when a person is approaching death, that you know where they are headed?”
He then replied:
"That person cannot even be known, much less their destination.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Then you may assemble and preach the Dharma.
Mañjuśrī said,
"Who wishes to listen?"
The Buddha said,
"Those who wish to listen may assemble.
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha:
"By means of what dharma is there anything to be spoken?
The Buddha said:
"I speak of the Dharma-body."
Mañjuśrī then said:
"If the Dharma-body is not seen, how can it be explained?
The Buddha spoke to Mañjuśrī:
“If the Dharma-body as it has been taught is invisible, those present in this assembly who do not yet understand will feel fear upon hearing these words.
Mañjuśrī said:
“If they feel fear, their fundamental limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) has already been terrified.”
The Buddha said:
"The primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi) is without fear; those who have not yet awakened are likewise without fear.
Mañjuśrī said:
"All phenomena are without fear, like a vajra.
The Buddha asked:
"What is meant by 'vajra'?"
He replied:
"There is nothing capable of cutting it off; for this reason, it is called 'Vajra.
The Buddha is inconceivable, and all dharmas are likewise inconceivable; for this reason, they are called 'Vajra.'"
The Buddha asked,
"What is it that constitutes a vajra?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"Because he is victorious over all phenomena, and because the Buddha is the ultimate realization of every dharma, he is called 'Vajra'.
[The questioner asks: "For what reason is the Buddha Vajra?
To which he replies:
"All that exists is non-existent; when each and every thing is sought, it is found to be non-existent, and is therefore called 'emptiness.
This emptiness is the Buddha, and for this reason it is the Vajra."
"All dharmas are the Buddha; because they rely upon no reliance, they are therefore vajra.
[The interlocutor asks: "For what reason is this called vajra? He then says:
"Because that which has no basis has nothing to approach, it is therefore called 'Vajra'.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Now I wish to manifest a response and cause Ānanda to come."
"Why is this? It is for the sake of all phenomena that are received.
Mañjuśrī asked the Buddha:
“Regarding the Dharma that has been taught, there is nothing to be seen and nothing to be attained; when Ānanda comes, what Dharma should he take?
The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent!”
"It is as Mañjuśrī has said.
The Buddha said:
"I see that in the countless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands of the eastern direction, all the Buddhas likewise proclaim this."
Śāriputra left his dwelling and went to where Mañjuśrī was; not finding him there, he proceeded to the Buddha’s location and stood outside the gate.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī,
“Call Śāriputra in.
Mañjuśrī then asked the Buddha:
“The fundamental limit, the Dharma-body—does it have a middle, an exterior, or an interior? From where could it be obtained?
The Buddha said:
“It cannot be obtained.”
He replied:
"The original limit is itself without limit.
He spoke again:
“Śāriputra is also within the Dharma-body; he has no place from which he comes, nor any place into which he enters.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
“If you are suffering, Śāriputra is not suffering.”
"It is as if various śrāvakas were conversing with me while inside, yet they were staying outside and did not enter at the improper time;
this would not be a nuisance. He replied, "Even though they stay outside, it is neither painful nor a nuisance."
The Buddha asked:
"For what reason are you neither distressed nor troubled?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“The Buddha preached the Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas, and I do likewise; therefore, I feel neither suffering nor vexation.
Why is this? Because it is the dharmakāya from which all Buddhas are detached.”
Mañjuśrī said:
"For example, even if one does not see the Buddha for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, nor gains entry [to his presence], one neither suffers nor is distressed.
Why is this? Because the Dharma taught by the Buddha neither increases nor decreases."
Why is this so? Because all dharmas have no master; for this reason, there is neither suffering nor vexation.
Whatever names exist, the Buddha employs them to teach people.
"Why is this? It is because the Buddha teaches by means of this.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra from afar:
“Did you hear all that Mañjuśrī said?
Śāriputra replied, “Indeed, Blessed One, do not trouble yourself; I wish to go there gladly to listen to his Dharma.”
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying,
"Please have Śāriputra come in.
The Buddha called out from afar for Śāriputra to approach.
Having approached, they paid their respects and took their seats.
Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra,
"In this Dharma, what is it that you hold as supreme, that you wish to enter and listen to?"
“I have heard it said that the Honored Dharma is worthy of love and delight; therefore, I have come desiring to hear it.
Mañjuśrī replied, “If it is indeed as you say, this Dharma is truly Honored, most profound, and exceedingly deep.”
Why is this? Because these dharmas possess no dualistic mind. For what reason?
It is not as you understand it; [the Dharma] is not contained therein. It is the same for all arhats and pratyekabuddhas, as well as those who seek the path of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because it is unattainable, nor is it obtained through longing; for this reason, nothing can exist within it.
Because it is fundamentally pure, all phenomena are also pure.
Śāriputra asked Mañjuśrī,
“Why is it that the Arhats are not included therein?
Mañjuśrī replied:
“When lust and anger are exhausted, one is an Arhat; having no dwelling place and nothing to be accomplished, where could such a person be?
Śāriputra said:
“I did not see him when I went to his location; for this reason I have come here to hear [of him], desiring only to hear the profound Dharma.”
Śāriputra said:
"Whether from the Buddha or from others, I have never grown weary of hearing his Dharma.
Mañjuśrī said:
"One never tires of the Dharma, just as Śāriputra has said.
Mañjuśrī asked:
"Can the Dharmakāya receive any dharma?"
"For what reason is there no weariness?
Śāriputra replied,
"The Dharma-body is without that which is received."
“Does that original limit have anything that is received?
Śāriputra replied,
“There is nothing received.”
Mañjuśrī replied to Śāriputra:
"Because the primordial limit (pūrvakoṭi) is without anything received, one never experiences weariness.
Mañjuśrī said:
“If you were to receive the Dharma from the very beginning, would you feel weary or exhausted?
Śāriputra replied,
“Aside from what the Buddha has spoken, there is nothing among my own words that can equal it.”
Mañjuśrī said:
"Can you have confidence in your own dharma as reaching nirvāṇa, or can you have confidence in it as not reaching nirvāṇa?
Śāriputra replied:
"From the very beginning, all have entered parinirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Can you truly believe that you are always thus, unwavering and unchanging?"
Śāriputra said, "I believe.
He asked again:
"If one asks, 'From what does this faith arise? the answer is:
'Because the Dharmakāya is neither produced nor extinguished, one knows it is without movement or change.'"
He asked again:
"Do you believe that Arhats have exhausted all [defilements] without remainder and have nothing further to know?
Śāriputra replied:
“Faith. “In what does one have faith?

“One knows that there is nothing further to exist; therefore, there is no object of knowledge. That which has no object of knowledge has no place of rest; therefore, it is called ‘exhaustion’ (kṣaya).”
Mañjuśrī said:
"The Arhats are thus because they have reached their end; for what reason?
Śāriputra replied:
"Because all dharmas are completely relinquished and nothing is apprehended.
Mañjuśrī asked:
"Do you believe that the Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have entered parinirvāṇa or have not entered parinirvāṇa?"
Śāriputra said, "I believe.
[The Buddha asked,] "In what do you believe?"
"Because the Dharma-body is neither born nor does it die, it does not enter parinirvāṇa.
Mañjuśrī asked:
"Do you believe that all Buddhas are one Buddha?"
Śāriputra said, “I believe.
“In what do you place your belief?”
He replied:
"Because the single Dharma-body is without duality.
Mañjuśrī asked:
"Do you believe that all existing buddha-fields are a single buddha-field?
Śāriputra replied,
"I believe so."
“From what does one have faith?
He replied, “Because all that exists has been exhausted.”
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Can one believe that all dharmas are without cognition, without liberation, without thought, and without realization?
Śāriputra replied:
“Faith. “In what does one have faith?

“One knows the spontaneous through spontaneity; therefore, there is no cognition, no liberation, no thought, and no realization. It is neither born nor extinguished, neither seen nor a seer. Since the primordial limit has no location, for this reason one has faith.”
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Does one who has faith abide in the Dharmakāya, which is without arising, without cessation, and without dwelling?
Śāriputra replied:
“I have faith.
“In what do you place your faith?
“I have faith because it is not a dharma that arises, ceases, or comes to rest.”
Mañjuśrī asked:
"Can one believe that the immeasurable Dharmakāya has its origin, and can one know its location?
Śāriputra replied:
"Faith. "In what does one have faith?
He replied:
"Because the Dharma-body is likewise free from lust, anger, and delusion, one has no place to rely upon when believing in it.
He then asked Śāriputra:
"Do you believe that all dharmas, the Buddha, and non-reliance are equal?"
He replied, “I believe it. [The other asked,] “On what basis do you believe it?”
He replied:
"There is no place of abiding.
That which has no place of abiding refers to that which relies upon the invisible."
Mañjuśrī said:
“Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!”
“If such are the realms [of your knowledge], I shall inquire about them all, and you shall answer each according to what you know.
Śāriputra said to Mañjuśrī,
“What I have heard now, I shall not forget through my mindfulness.”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"If there are men or women who hear this Dharma, uphold, recite, and read it, and explain its meaning in detail for all people, they will swiftly attain what they desire."
Mañjuśrī said to Śāriputra,
"What the Buddha has now spoken is no different [from what was said before].
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“Those who made offerings to the Buddhas of the past have all come to obtain this seal.
What is the name of this Dharma?
How should it be practiced?”

"Its names are 'Inquiry into the Dharmakāya,' 'Jewel Accumulation,' 'Upholding the Ultimate Limit,' and 'Upholding the Non-abiding. That which it upholds sustains all dharmas without any obstruction."
Those who hear this from others will, by means of this Dharma, all attain it; those who have heard it shall further instruct and admonish others, leading and guiding one another in succession.
"Why is this? Because the text is brief, yet the understanding it yields is vast.

When the Buddha had spoken this sutra, Śāriputra and the arhats, Mañjuśrī and the bodhisattvas, as well as all the devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits of the world, were filled with joy; they paid their respects and departed.
The Sutra on the Dharmakāya Spoken by the Buddha as Requested by Mañjuśrī in the Ratnakūṭa Samādhi.
